entry.summary: Creative Insight The rise of the employee creator Employee-generated content is evolving beyond brand advocacy. CR explores the value of staff developing their own followings and identities, and the challenges this presents for brands By Rebecca Fulleylove 12/11/2026 3:52 am From
entry.content:
Creative Insight

The rise of the employee creator

Employee-generated content is evolving beyond brand advocacy. CR explores the value of staff developing their own followings and identities, and the challenges this presents for brands

By Rebecca Fulleylove 12/11/2026 3:52 am

From M&S’s director of product development Kathryn Turner to Kaeden Rowland, the deadpan print specialist better known as the Staples Baddie, employees are becoming some of the most interesting new brand storytellers.
Waitrose, Hobbycraft and Waterstones’ local store accounts are also racking up views, while Starbucks and Gap have announced developments to their employee creator initiatives. It seems brands are happily looking inwards for a new generation of creative talent.

Employee-generated content (EGC) isn’t new, but what’s evolved is the ambition and creativity behind it. Rather than simply asking staff to share corporate messaging, brands are beginning to recognise employees as creators with the potential to build audiences around their own expertise and personalities.

But as staff build audiences and identities beyond their day jobs, brands face a new challenge. How much freedom are they prepared to give the people who represent them?

entry.title: Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school The hand-drawn branding for Istanbul-based Güneş Ülkesi has been designed to reflect both its name and evolving cultural role By Adam Woodward 12/11/2026 3:26 am Turkish creative studio Garip St
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school

The hand-drawn branding for Istanbul-based Güneş Ülkesi has been designed to reflect both its name and evolving cultural role

By Adam Woodward 12/11/2026 3:26 am

Turkish creative studio Garip Studio has developed a colourful, hand-drawn identity for Güneş Ülkesi, a school that encourages children to explore the arts through movement, experimentation and play.

Founded in 2019, Güneş Ülkesi teaches ballet, music, painting and creative drama, primarily to children under the age of ten. Its approach encourages pupils to move freely between disciplines, building confidence while developing their own ways of seeing and making. As the school looks to expand its reach and bring more children into the arts, it wanted an identity that could reflect its ambitions and evolving cultural role.

The resulting visual identity takes its starting point from the school’s name, which translates as ‘Land of the Sun’. At its centre is a custom logotype, drawn entirely by hand and arranged in a circular composition to resemble a sun.

Rather than functioning simply as a wordmark, the lettering becomes the identity’s primary visual device, informing everything from printed materials to digital communications and the school’s physical spaces.

The colour palette follows the same solar inspiration, combining bright yellow, warm orange and soft beige, with black marks introduced according to context. Halyard Display by Darden Studio provides a more restrained typographic counterpoint to the expressive lettering.

The identity also incorporates a series of animated elements, with individual motion pieces developed for each of the school’s disciplines. Lesson animations, inspired by the typography, are used to announce classes, while the lettering’s variable, free-flowing character allows the wider system to be continually reinterpreted across the school’s activities and performances.

For Bertuğ Bilgin, founder and creative director of Garip Studio, the aim was to capture something of the uninhibited imagination that defines childhood. “The sun is one of the first things almost every child draws. We built the identity around that, and around the uninhibited imagination of the children themselves,” he says.

He adds: “We wanted the lettering to do more than sign off the brand. It gives the whole identity its movement, rhythm and sense of play, so it feels as free as the children who learn there.”

entry.title: Bolt transforms scooters into trackers of urban accessibility
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Bolt transforms scooters into trackers of urban accessibility Utilising existing sensors on their e-scooters, Bolt is recording the quality of street surfaces to help improve the lives of wheelchair users By Daniel Milroy Maher 12/11/2026 3:01 am For the 80 m
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Bolt transforms scooters into trackers of urban accessibility

Utilising existing sensors on their e-scooters, Bolt is recording the quality of street surfaces to help improve the lives of wheelchair users

By Daniel Milroy Maher 12/11/2026 3:01 am

For the 80 million people across the world who use wheelchairs to get around, navigating city streets can pose more challenges than simply knowing which direction to go in. Though wheelchair technology has improved significantly in recent years, all wheelchair users remain at the mercy of street-level surface quality. Shoddy paving, cobblestones and other uneven surfaces present health and safety risks to those who are forced to ride over them.

Recently, European shared mobility platform Bolt realised that this issue extended beyond wheelchair users, and even affected customers who choose to use their iconic green scooters for transport. Scooter wheels, as much as wheelchair wheels, struggle with uneven terrain, and make for an uncomfortable journey for the rider. For wheelchair users in particular, they can actually cause chronic pain, from the body being repeatedly jolted around.

Which is why Bolt has worked with Serviceplan Group on a clever new initiative called Wheels4Wheels, which repurposes sensors already attached to Bolt scooters to collect accessibility data that many mainstream maps are unable to provide. This data, which offers a much-needed insight into surface quality on streets all over Europe, is being made publicly accessible so that any navigation service, city authority, or developer can use it for free.

“Every year, our scooters cover millions of kilometres across hundreds of cities, registering every bump, slope, and uneven surface along the way,” explains Ardo Reinsalu, director of vehicles at Bolt. “We have long shared that data with city partners to help improve roads and pavements for everyone. Wheels4Wheels takes that a step further by making the same information available directly to the people who need it most – without building a new app, but improving the maps they already use.”

To promote the project, Bolt worked with Serviceplan Group to create a campaign that emphasises the importance of freely sharing this data, and how it can improve quality of life for millions of people. In a short film, adventurous wheelchair user Hendra explains how getting around her city is often made difficult due to a lack of accessibility information. She explains that having the kind of data that Bolt has collected at her fingertips would be “a game-changer”, transforming scooters into something that would “finally be useful” for her.

Following a successful trial period in Tallinn, Estonia, during which time Bolt scooters covered 550km across all eight city districts, and produced 66,088 individual surface ratings (and increased available surface-quality information by 26%), Wheels4Wheels is being rolled out in cities all around Europe. The resulting data will be published to OpenStreetMap, the world’s largest open-source map database, from where it can be automatically integrated into apps that support surface-based routing.

Alex Schill, global CCO at Serviceplan Group, concludes: “Wheels4Wheels shows how an existing platform can be reimagined as civic infrastructure. What began as mobility data for fleet operations becomes a practical tool for inclusion, turning a familiar urban service into an open resource for more accessible cities. We’re very proud to support a matter that hopefully improves the daily lives of thousands of people.”

entry.title: A new book captures the strange beauty of decaying outdoor advertising
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration A new book captures the strange beauty of decaying outdoor advertising Accidental Collage sees Manchester design studio Dr.Me document six years of torn posters, celebrating the art of looking beyond the intended message By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 3:55 am Ou
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

A new book captures the strange beauty of decaying outdoor advertising

Accidental Collage sees Manchester design studio Dr.Me document six years of torn posters, celebrating the art of looking beyond the intended message

By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 3:55 am

Outdoor advertising is designed to grab our attention, but what happens when the message starts to fall apart? Posters are ripped down, billboards succumb to the weather and layers of old campaigns emerge beneath newer ones, creating unexpected compositions that their original designers could never have anticipated.

These chance encounters are the subject of Accidental Collage, a new book by Manchester-based design studio Dr.Me, which collects six years of photographs documenting the unintended visual arrangements found on streets around the world.

The project began in February 2020 as a personal photography archive for Mark Edwards, who co-founded Dr.Me with Ryan Doyle in 2010. As the studio travelled internationally for design events, workshops and exhibitions, Edwards began noticing the visual possibilities of decaying advertising, from Paris to London to New York.

The pandemic subsequently changed the project’s trajectory. With international travel curtailed, Edwards began exploring Manchester by bicycle, documenting neglected advertising hoardings and posters that had been left to deteriorate. One particularly memorable billboard gradually peeled away from an ad for Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds, revealing an old McDonald’s campaign beneath it. Edwards dubbed the resulting combination ‘NickDonald’s and the bad seeds’.

As the archive grew, Accidental Collage evolved into a collaborative project, attracting contributions from artists and creatives around the world. Among them are fine artist and musician Hisham Akira Bharoocha, graphic artist and book designer Sarah Boris, graphic designer Nick Deakin and drummer Jeremy Gustin, who documented found compositions while touring with musicians including David Byrne, Joan as Police Woman and Iggy Pop.

For Bharoocha, who began photographing torn posters in the early 2000s, the appeal lies in the unexpected relationships between images. “The stranger the juxtaposition the merrier,” he says, describing how fragments of advertisements can combine to create entirely unplanned visual narratives.

The results also offer a different way of thinking about authorship. Who creates an accidental collage: the person who puts up the poster, the passer-by who tears it down or the photographer who recognises its potential? In an accompanying essay, Boris describes the works as “a collective endeavour, shaped by countless hands, moments and colours”.

The book also arrives at a time when the physical advertising landscape is changing. “I’ve come to think about ‘accidental collage’ as the biggest free ever-changing art show,” says Edwards. “With the rise of digital advertising, however, they’re becoming less frequent in cities and discoverable in less well-heeled areas.”

In Manchester, he notes, the turnover of advertising has accelerated, leaving less time for weather and passers-by to transform the surfaces. Yet construction hoardings and neglected streets continue to offer opportunities for discovery.

Rather than simply repurposing these images in his own design work, Edwards approaches them more like an archaeologist documenting a find. The project has, however, influenced his practice, including experiments with torn typography and adhesive tape.

Written and designed by Dr.Me, with essays and contributions from its collaborators, Accidental Collage makes a strong case for paying closer attention to our surroundings – and for finding new creative possibilities in the often overlooked details of everyday life.

Accidental Collage is published by Waiting Room press; waitingroom.press

entry.content:
Creative Insight

How A24 ripped up the film brand rulebook

From indie distributor to fashion-adjacent cultural force, A24 keeps on reimagining what a film company can be. Here, we explore recent campaigns for the likes of Primetime and You Can See Everything, as well as its partnership with Dior

By Adam Woodward 11/11/2026 3:07 am

There was a time not so long ago when A24 was shorthand for a certain kind of indie film. The New York-based company emerged in 2012 as a distributor with an eye for picking up projects that sat outside the mainstream – typically slightly leftfield, artist-led films with, it must be said, somewhat limited appeal.

It helped that the company could count the likes of Sofia Coppola and Harmony Korine among its early roster of directors, but in purely business terms, it was still a relatively small, niche-interest proposition.

Since then, thanks to a string of critical and commercial hits including Moonlight, Hereditary, Midsommar, Uncut Gems and Everything Everywhere All at Once, A24 has steadily grown into one of the world’s leading entertainment brands. Yet the most striking aspect of A24’s rise has been the creative evolution of the brand itself.

entry.title: Feminist graphic design takes centre stage at new exhibition
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Feminist graphic design takes centre stage at new exhibition London’s Saatchi Gallery is celebrating the radical protest art of 70s print collective See Red Women’s Workshop as part of its Beyond the Streets show By Adam Woodward 11/11/2026 3:05 am When See R
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Feminist graphic design takes centre stage at new exhibition

London’s Saatchi Gallery is celebrating the radical protest art of 70s print collective See Red Women’s Workshop as part of its Beyond the Streets show

By Adam Woodward 11/11/2026 3:05 am

When See Red Women’s Workshop was founded in London in 1974, its members wanted to challenge the way women were represented in advertising and the media. More than 50 years later, the feminist print collective’s bold, often humorous posters continue to resonate, with a selection of its work set to feature in Beyond the Streets at Saatchi Gallery.

The posters featured in the exhibition, which explores six decades of street culture, art and activism, demonstrate how graphic design became an important tool for the women’s liberation movement, turning everyday experiences of sexism and inequality into striking visual statements.

“Rampant sexism permeated all aspects of women’s lives when we started in the 70s,” say founding members Pru Stevenson, Suzy Mackie and Anne Robinson. “Women’s bodies were exploited, abused and exposed, being used to sell everything from cars to toilet paper.”

Working with bold colours, collage, hand-drawn imagery and sharp slogans, See Red tackled a range of subjects including domestic labour, childcare, sexuality, racism and lesbian visibility. One poster depicted a woman trapped inside a pill bottle, while another showed various women partaking in physical work and leisure activities traditionally associated with men.

Humour also played its part. The members wanted to produce images that people would actively choose to display in their homes, rather than simply functional campaign material. “No one wants to live with a relentlessly depressing image,” they tell CR. “Humour became an important part of our work and it was a way of presenting ideas in an accessible way, encouraging many women to challenge the status quo.”

The collective also sought to challenge the traditional hierarchies of the art world. Having studied at art school during the 1960s and early 70s, its founders had become frustrated by a culture that celebrated the individual artist, often at the expense of collaboration. Instead, See Red operated without hierarchy or individual credits, with ideas discussed, revised and developed collectively before being printed.

“All the tasks associated with running a screen printing workshop were shared by everyone,” the founders say. Sharing technical knowledge was equally important, with members teaching other women how to screen print at conferences and meetings, helping them produce their own campaign materials.

Around 45 women passed through the workshop during its lifetime. Initially based in a Camden squat before relocating to south London, See Red relied on poster sales, community commissions and donations to keep going. Its work also attracted hostility from the far right, with repeated attacks by the National Front resulting in smashed doors, damaged machinery and cut telephone lines. Despite the intimidation and financial pressures, See Red continued until the workshop closed in 1990.

More than a quarter of a century later, its legacy lives on. The collective has been recognised through several major exhibitions in recent years, including Tate Britain’s Women in Revolt! Art and Activism in the UK 1970-1990 in 2023-24, a dedicated show at San Francisco’s Haight Street Art Center in 2024-25, and now at London’s Saatchi Gallery.

For the founders, the renewed interest in their work, particularly among younger feminists, reflects both its enduring visual appeal and the continued relevance of its subject matter. “The posters seem able to speak to different generations,” they say, “although it indicates, as if we were in any doubt, that the struggle for women’s freedom and equality is far from won.”

They are also keen to emphasise the enduring value of working together in a physical sense. “The ability to make contact with other artists and activists globally … is hugely positive for anyone seeking to challenge societal injustices or set up campaigns. However, this is set against an online culture largely controlled by capitalist corporations, the ‘echo chamber’ effects of social media and the toxicity and polarisation which has also developed,” they say.

“Meeting in person, face to face and especially creating work together, may cut through division and enhance the possibility for exchanges of ideas – and the material quality of silkscreen printing is distinctive.”

Beyond the Streets runs at Saatchi Gallery until May 5, 2027; saatchigallery.com

entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Netflix celebrates the thrill of the binge in cinematic new campaign Netflix’s new brand platform, Find The Thing You Never Knew You Needed, embraces all of its obsessive viewers out there By Daniel Milroy Maher 10/11/2026 1:00 pm Netflix has launched a new c
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Netflix celebrates the thrill of the binge in cinematic new campaign

Netflix’s new brand platform, Find The Thing You Never Knew You Needed, embraces all of its obsessive viewers out there

By Daniel Milroy Maher 10/11/2026 1:00 pm

Netflix has launched a new campaign built around the moments of serendipity that many of its users experience while browsing the platform for something to watch. Developed through a collaboration between Netflix’s Brand Creative Studio and creative agency Mother, Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed celebrates captivating storytelling and the joy of discovery.

Tapping into real user behaviour, the creative teams chose to capture the thrill of falling in love with a new show through a series of three short spots, all directed by award-winning director duo Vania & Muggia. Beautifully shot on 35mm film, each of the spots is presented in a different aspect ratio.

Axolotl reveals the great lengths a brave amphibian will go to to keep its beloved Bridgerton marathon alive; Dawn follows a Love Is Blind-addicted vampire as he withstands the effects of the sun to keep watching his show; and in Hypersleep a lonely astronaut prematurely wakes his crewmate from their stasis chamber slumber to share the plot of KPop Demon Hunters.

These stories are enhanced by immersive set design (each taking weeks to build) and sound design, including the claustrophobic silence of space and upbeat tracks such as A.I.E by Roberta Kelly.

“People come to Netflix trusting they’ll discover something new to love, often something they didn’t see coming,” says Aarti Thiagarajan, senior director at the Brand Creative Studio. “We wanted to celebrate that moment when you get hooked. So we started with the things real fans do, like staying up for one more episode or blowing up the group chat about a new obsession, and turned them into a campaign as entertaining as the shows and films that inspire them.”

Find The Thing You Never Knew You Needed launched this week in the US, Canada, Brazil and Spain, with more countries to follow.

entry.title: Waitrose reunites Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for The Perfect Gift 2
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Waitrose reunites Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for The Perfect Gift 2 Created by Wonderhood Studios, this year’s festive campaign is a nearly six-minute romantic epic about the power of love – and good pastry – at Christmas By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 10
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Waitrose reunites Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for The Perfect Gift 2

Created by Wonderhood Studios, this year’s festive campaign is a nearly six-minute romantic epic about the power of love – and good pastry – at Christmas

By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 10:06 am

Not to be outdone by its department store stable mate, Waitrose has once again brought out the big guns for its latest Christmas campaign.

The supermarket has reunited Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for The Perfect Gift 2, a six-minute festive rom-com that picks up where last year’s story left off. This time, however, there are new obstacles to love in the shape of a wedding, a rival suitor and a rather large beef wellington.

Knightley reprises her role as herself, while Wilkinson returns as Phil “Phil Phil”, the everyman who charmed her over the Waitrose cheese counter last Christmas. Twelve months on, Knightley is now engaged to the suave, self-absorbed and improbably named Hugo Bunty-Griffin (Alex Hassell), although she doesn’t appear entirely happy about it.

Cue a heartbroken Phil, whose friends hatch a plan to help him win Keira back. With just hours until the ceremony, he sets about making a homemade beef wellington from scratch (surely there are less time-consuming romantic gestures?) in a last-ditch bid to remind her where her heart really belongs. A nice timely jilting ensues, with pastry providing the unlikely key to true love.

At just under six minutes, the film is reportedly the longest Christmas ad ever produced by a UK supermarket, surpassing last year’s effort with an even more elaborate cinematic plot. Snow-covered country houses, sweeping crane shots and an orchestral score recorded by the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra give the production the full Hollywood treatment, while Jennifer Rush’s The Power of Love provides an appropriately grand finale.

Created by Wonderhood Studios and produced by Biscuit Filmworks, the campaign sees director Molly Manners return to the helm, whose other credits include the Netflix series One Day. As with last year’s instalment, Waitrose is borrowing heavily from the language of the movies to give the ad a longer life beyond the traditional TV spot. Although its length does mean it risks outstaying its welcome, it certainly isn’t short of the right ingredients.

entry.title: Penguin launches new Twentieth-Century Classics hardback editions
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Penguin launches new Twentieth-Century Classics hardback editions From East of Eden to The Outsider, some of the century’s most notable titles have been released as photography-led hardback editions for this new collection By Daniel Milroy Maher 10/11/2026 3:
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Penguin launches new Twentieth-Century Classics hardback editions

From East of Eden to The Outsider, some of the century’s most notable titles have been released as photography-led hardback editions for this new collection

By Daniel Milroy Maher 10/11/2026 3:23 am

Penguin Classics has launched Twentieth-Century Classics, a new hardback library featuring seminal works of literature from this rich and fertile period of publishing. Inspired by the established visual language of Penguin Modern Classics, this latest collection spotlights the iconic photographs that have come to symbolise these treasured titles.

Set for a staggered release, the first five volumes in the Twentieth-Century Classics collection have been revealed: East of Eden by John Steinbeck, In Cold Blood by Truman Capote, The Heart is a Lonely Hunter by Carson McCullers, The Outsider by Albert Camus, and The Spy Who Came in from the Cold by John le Carré.

Bound in a beautiful and tactile eau-de-nil cloth, a colour that has long adorned Penguin Modern Classics books, these titles also feature photographs that have been inset into a debossed panel on the front, as well as lettering stamped in black foil. Inside, modern text settings ensure these defining works are made accessible to readers, while soft, uncoated Munken paper promises a comfortable read.

While every aspect of these new releases has been carefully considered, the photography is where the books really shine. Originally chosen by the Penguin Classics team to represent these influential works of literature, the imagery is now taking centre stage, having served as enduring symbols that draw readers in as much as the titles of the books themselves.

“Penguin has always accompanied great writing with great art,” notes Jim Stoddart, art director at Penguin Press. “Penguin Modern Classics in particular has long championed cover photography. With these new hardback editions, we’ve taken this tradition a step further.”

On the cover of The Heart is a Lonely Hunter, for instance, an image by Ukrainian photographer Jack Delano perfectly encapsulates the themes of the book – namely human isolation and the system injustices of the American South. Delano’s photograph of a black man standing by himself at a county fair effortlessly transports readers to that time and place.

Commenting on the union of McCullers and Delano’s work in this edition of the novel, Sam Johnson, picture editor at Penguin Press, says: “Carson McCullers was praised for her ‘astonishing humanity’ in this debut novel, [which she wrote] at the age of 23, and I can see this same strength in the photographs of Jack Delano, who wrote that ‘to do justice to the subject has always been my main concern.’”

The other featured photographers in the current collection are Walker Evans, Richard Avedon, Rankin, and Henri Cartier-Bresson, with five more to come in the second release of Twentieth-Century Classics titles in April 2027. The next batch includes renowned Swiss-American photographer Robert Frank, whose image of two young men in a car adorns the front cover of On the Road by Jack Kerouac.

entry.title: How the Nordics are turning tourism advertising on its head
entry.summary: Creative Insight How the Nordics are turning tourism advertising on its head A new wave of destination marketing is swapping familiar travel clichés for irreverence, self-deprecation and culturally distinctive creative ideas By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 3:00 am From dramatic fjord
entry.content:
Creative Insight

How the Nordics are turning tourism advertising on its head

A new wave of destination marketing is swapping familiar travel clichés for irreverence, self-deprecation and culturally distinctive creative ideas

By Adam Woodward 10/11/2026 3:00 am

From dramatic fjords and rugged archipelagos to the northern lights and the promise of a sauna whenever you need one, the Nordics have no shortage of reason to visit. But as competition for travellers’ attention intensifies, tourist boards are finding increasingly inventive ways to sell the Scandi dream. Many are embracing ironic humour, self-deprecation and unexpected cultural connections to create memorable campaigns.

Over the past year or so, some of the best examples have included Visit Sweden’s Introvert Travel Agency and The Swedish Prescription, as well as Icelandair’s not-AI campaign and its search for the world’s best Really Bad Photographer. Finland, meanwhile, has been busy promoting the Turku Archipelago as ‘the best-smelling destination in the world’, and inviting Pamela Anderson to reclaim her Finnish heritage, with the help of local creative agency United Imaginations.

Across the region, a particular strain of irreverent destination marketing has emerged. Of course, there are many differences between the countries, both geographically and culturally, but a willingness to poke fun at themselves, challenge expectations and find unconventional ways into wider cultural conversations appears to be a common thread.

entry.title: Disney saddles up for a little Christmas magic in festive short
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Disney saddles up for a little Christmas magic in festive short Directed by Dougal Wilson, The Invisible Horse follows a boy who thinks he’s outgrown Christmas magic, until an unexpected visitor reignites his imagination By Rebecca Fulleylove 09/11/2026 1:00
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Disney saddles up for a little Christmas magic in festive short

Directed by Dougal Wilson, The Invisible Horse follows a boy who thinks he’s outgrown Christmas magic, until an unexpected visitor reignites his imagination

By Rebecca Fulleylove 09/11/2026 1:00 pm

Disney has tapped into the power of imagination for its Christmas campaign, unveiling a new festive short, The Invisible Horse, directed by Dougal Wilson and created by agency adam&eve\TBWA.

The film centres on Jack, a young boy who has seemingly outgrown the magic of Christmas. But when an invisible companion rocks up at his house, he finds himself swept into an adventure that reignites his imagination and brings him closer to his family.

While last year’s spot, directed by Taika Waititi, focused on the joy of giving, this time the emphasis is on the idea that the magic of Christmas is less about the things we receive and more about what we believe in.

As you’d expect from Disney, the film dances close to schmaltz, but perhaps thanks to Wilson’s direction, it manages to avoid tipping into anything too sickly sweet.

Instead, there’s a sense of playfulness and charm that allows the central relationship to take centre stage, giving the story an emotional pull without labouring its message. The presence of Jack’s frowny, discerning little sister helps keep the sentiment in check, too.

The short marks the launch of Disney’s global Make the Holidays Magic campaign, which brings together entertainment, experiences and gifting under one seasonal platform. The initiative also puts a focus on giving back, with Disney continuing its support for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.

Through the campaign, Disney will look to raise awareness and funds for the charity, as well as create special surprises and experiences for children and families across the UK and Ireland through its wish-granting programme at Disneyland Paris.

It’s a familiar festive formula – imagination, family and a little bit of magic – but one that Disney knows how to deliver. And with Wilson at the helm, the result feels more like an endearing Christmas story than an overly extended brand advert.

entry.title: Morrisons reworks a classic fairy tale for its Christmas campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Morrisons reworks a classic fairy tale for its Christmas campaign Created by Leo UK, the ad is a modern reworking of Goldilocks and the Three Bears and a refreshingly different festive ad campaign By Eliza Williams 09/11/2026 3:39 am This year’s Christmas adv
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Morrisons reworks a classic fairy tale for its Christmas campaign

Created by Leo UK, the ad is a modern reworking of Goldilocks and the Three Bears and a refreshingly different festive ad campaign

By Eliza Williams 09/11/2026 3:39 am

This year’s Christmas advertising has featured plenty of traditional festive scenes, with a heavy emphasis on luxury. Sprawling country homes, twinkly lights and gifts a-plenty have appeared across many ads.

So this spot for Morrisons supermarket stands out for its unexpected reworking of Goldilocks and the Three Bears, and for portraying a family that is perhaps not entirely looking forward to the upcoming festive season.

A curmudgeonly pair of bear parents are shown being thrown into a flat spin when their son announces he is bringing his new partner home for the first time at Christmas. Happily Morrisons is on hand to provide plenty of fresh food that is prepared just to the various bears (and their visitor’s) individual tastes.

The ad is directed by Nick Ball, who brings both wit and complex craft to the ad. The suits for the bears are seven feet tall and operated with actors inside them doing the body movements, while intricate animatronics are used for the faces, operated by puppeteers. The bears’ house was custom built to be large enough to contain them.

The campaign includes the 90-second TV spot and also a week-long Instagram takeover, which tells Baby Bear and Goldilocks’ side of the story, following their journey home through Gen Z style photo dumps, short videos and Stories, including a ‘not too hard, not too soft’ launch of their relationship. In addition, nationwide out-of-home executions further the story of the Bears through candid photos from their Christmas.

“There’s a huge amount of craft in bringing a family everyone knows to life and giving each bear their own personality,” says Andrew Long, CCO at Leo UK. “Goldilocks and the Three Bears is a story generations know, but people experience stories very differently today. So we’ve built the campaign to work in different ways too: each generation gets its own way into the story.”

Credits:
Agency: Leo UK
CCO: Andrew Long
